function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
**Triangulation metrics** are quantitative measures that describe the *quality*, *characteristics*, and *performance* of a triangulation—i.e., a division of a domain (often a plane or surface) into triangles. They are used in many fields—computer graphics, finite‑element analysis, GIS terrain modeling, mesh generation, and computational geometry—to evaluate how well a triangulation satisfies desired criteria and to compare different triangulation algorithms or meshes. Below is a concise overview of the most common categories of triangulation metrics and why they matter. | Category | Typical Metric(s) | What it Measures | Why It Matters | |----------|------------------|------------------|----------------| | **Geometric Quality** | • Minimum/maximum angle
• Aspect ratio (ratio of longest side to shortest altitude)
• Radius‑edge ratio (circumradius / shortest edge)
• Edge length distribution | Shape regularity of individual triangles | Poorly shaped triangles (e.g., skinny or obtuse) can lead to numerical instability in FEM, poor rendering, or inaccurate interpolation. | | **Size Distribution** | • Average triangle area
• Standard deviation of area
• Edge length histogram | How uniformly sized the triangles are | Uniform sizing often improves solver convergence and visual consistency; large variance may indicate over‑ or under‑refinement. | | **Conformity & Feature Preservation** | • Edge alignment error (difference between mesh edges and known feature lines)
• Feature‑preserving ratio (percentage of mesh edges that lie on a feature) | How well the mesh respects input constraints (e.g., boundaries, ridges) | Essential for accurate representation of complex geometries or terrain features. | | **Topological Properties** | • Connectivity count (number of neighboring triangles per vertex)
• Mesh genus (number of holes) | Topological correctness and consistency | Ensures the mesh is a valid manifold and that algorithms relying on topology (e.g., pathfinding) work correctly. | | **Performance Metrics** | • Runtime (seconds)
• Memory usage (MB)
• Number of iterations (for iterative refinement) | Computational cost of generating or refining the mesh | Important when scaling to large datasets or real‑time applications. | | **Accuracy / Fidelity** | • Hausdorff distance to ground truth surface
• Mean squared error (MSE) of interpolated values | How closely the mesh approximates the underlying surface or data | Critical for scientific visualization, terrain modeling, or any application where fidelity matters. | ### How These Metrics Are Used 1. **Mesh Generation & Refinement** - During mesh creation, algorithms often aim to maximize the minimum angle or minimize the radius‑edge ratio. - Refinement strategies adjust local triangle sizes to meet a target area or edge length. 2. **Quality Assurance** - After generation, a suite of metrics is computed to flag triangles that violate thresholds (e.g., aspect ratio > 10). - Automated reports help engineers quickly identify problematic regions. 3. **Algorithm Comparison** - By comparing metrics across different triangulation methods (Delaunay, constrained Delaunay, advancing front, etc.), developers can choose the best approach for their specific needs. 4. **Optimization & Tuning** - Metrics guide parameter tuning (e.g., tolerance levels, refinement depth) to balance quality against computational cost. 5. **Scientific Validation** - In GIS or terrain modeling, metrics such as the Hausdorff distance ensure that a TIN (Triangulated Irregular Network) accurately represents a DEM (Digital Elevation Model). ### Example: Delaunay Triangulation Metrics For a Delaunay triangulation, the following metrics are often reported: - **Minimum angle** – Delaunay tends to maximize this, reducing skinny triangles. - **Maximum angle** – Helps detect overly obtuse triangles that may still exist. - **Aspect ratio** – Indicates how close triangles are to equilateral. - **Edge length ratio** – Useful for detecting abrupt changes in mesh density. These metrics are typically computed per triangle and then aggregated (mean, median, percentiles) to give a global sense of mesh quality. --- In short, **triangulation metrics** provide a systematic way to quantify the shape, size, conformity, topology, performance, and fidelity of a triangulation. They are indispensable for ensuring that a mesh meets the requirements of the application at hand—whether that’s numerical simulation, visual rendering, or geographic analysis.
